query: Which method can be used for concurrent strength–ductility improvement, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Applying a machine learning (ML) workflow that correlates alloy compositions, processing parameters, and microstructures will enable the identification of new processing routes for high-entropy alloys that increase yield strength by at least 10–20% while maintaining or improving ductility above 10%.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-principal element (high-entropy) alloys in as-cast or partially processed form, which often show high strength but limited ductility.
generation.intervention: Train an ML model on existing datasets of alloy compositions, microstructures, and mechanical properties, then use it to recommend novel process parameters (e.g., thermal treatment steps and deformation schedules) for achieving enhanced strength–ductility synergy.
generation.conditions: Employ standard vacuum melting or powder consolidation methods followed by ML-guided multi-step heat treatments and/or mechanical processing, with systematic characterization to validate property improvements.
generation.structural_mediator: Fine-scale lamellar or precipitate-rich microstructures tailored by the ML-guided processing route, enabling balanced strain hardening and controlled dislocation slip.
generation.mechanism: ML-optimized processing refines and disperses coherent precipitates or dual-phase regions that inhibit crack initiation yet sustain dislocation activity, improving both tensile strength and elongation before failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Elevated yield strength (≥2 GPa or at least 10–20% above the baseline) while preserving or increasing tensile ductility beyond 10%.
generation.baseline: Typical equiatomic high-entropy alloys can reach ~2 GPa strength but often exhibit <10% elongation due to limited ductility from coarse or brittle phases.
generation.boundary: The ML model requires sufficiently diverse and accurate data on compositions and prior forging/heat treatment parameters; extrapolation beyond well-characterized composition ranges may incur risk of prediction errors.
generation.uncertainty: There is limited direct experimental validation for this ML approach, and further studies are needed to confirm generalizability and refine predictive power.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a set of novel equiatomic and near-equiatomic HEA compositions recommended by the ML workflow, produce test ingots via the same melting, casting, or sintering processes, and apply the predicted optimal thermal and mechanical treatments to achieve enhanced strength–ductility synergy.
measurements: Tensile stress–strain curves to quantify yield strength and ductility
Microstructural analysis via SEM/TEM to verify predicted microstructural features
X-ray diffraction to confirm phase constitution and precipitate formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If none of the ML-guided composition and processing routes produce statistically significant increases in yield strength (≥10%) along with ductility ≥10%, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

decision.trend: Early work (PMC4145285) showed that a fine lamellar dual-phase microstructure could deliver both high strength and ductility in an as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy. Later studies (PMC5995863) further demonstrated that careful control of phase stability via heat treatment could retain excellent strength while enhancing ductility in a once-brittle refractory high-entropy alloy. Most recently (PMC10213035), stepwise thermo-mechanical processing introduced multiple coherent precipitates that drive ultrahigh strength without sacrificing elongation, highlighting the critical role of tailored microstructure in overcoming the typical strength–ductility trade-off. While these efforts yield promising results, they generally require extensive trial-and-error experimentation due to the vast compositional and process parameter space.
decision.unsolved: A key challenge remains in systematically identifying and refining processing conditions to optimize strength–ductility synergy across various alloy systems. Despite advances in alloy design and microstructure engineering, a comprehensive and rapid design strategy to predict the most effective processing routes and microstructures for improved mechanical performance is still lacking.
decision.lever: Develop an ML-driven workflow that correlates processing pathways, microstructure features, and mechanical property outcomes to guide experiments for concurrent strength–ductility enhancements.
decision.why: Machine learning tools can rapidly explore wide design spaces, uncover hidden process–structure–property correlations, and propose promising new processing conditions. This accelerates innovation beyond iterative trial-and-error approaches and enables systematic optimization of both strength and ductility.
